lasswell-1927-propaganda.title: Propaganda technique in the World War
lasswell-1927-propaganda.publisher: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co.; Alfred A. Knopf

verified.note: Open Library lists the 1927 editions (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner; A. A. Knopf) and the 1938 Peter Smith reprint. OCR text of two scans read on archive.org: the 1927 London/New York edition (Delhi University Library copy, id dli.ernet.6011; title page 'London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., Ltd. New York: Alfred A. Knopf') and the 1938 Peter Smith reprint (id PropagandaTechniqueInTheWorldWar). Passages checked in both: p. 217 (Wilson, 'injected into the veins'), p. 220 ('one of the most powerful instrumentalities in the modern world'; difficulty of separating propaganda from other means of control), p. 221 ('new hammer and anvil of social solidarity'), p. 222 ('atomized world'; 'more can be won by illusion than by coercion'). Neither OCR text contains 'hypodermic', 'needle' or 'syringe'; 'bullet' occurs only in war-law lists, in a footnoted book title (Bullets and Billets, 1917) and in a quotation ('Thoughts are Bullets', attributed there to George William Curtis); 'magic' only in 'the magic of his eloquence'.

berlo-1960.title: The process of communication: An introduction to theory and practice

verified.note: Open Library lists the 1960 Holt, Rinehart and Winston edition (LCCN 60007981). schramm-roberts-1971.title: The process and effects of mass communication

verified.note: Open Library lists the 1971 revised edition (University of Illinois Press) and the 1954 first edition. Full-text PDF of the revised edition read (worldradiohistory.com copy): contents, foreword, the editors' introductions and the reprinted articles. On p. 59 the editors write of the 'long-held "hypodermic needle" or "bullet" theory of mass media effect' being doubted after the 1940 election study; their introduction to the audience section describes the Cooper-Jahoda 'Mr. Biggott' study.

pooley-socolow-2013-ijoc.title: Checking up on The Invasion from Mars: Hadley Cantril, Paul F. Lazarsfeld, and the making of a misremembered classic

verified.note: Open-access PDF read in full (ijoc.org, 29 pages; volume/pages as printed on the running heads). Used for: the 'hypodermic needle / magic bullet' shorthand and the textbook two-stage story; Lowery & DeFleur 1983 organisation; Stanton's Hooper Holmes questionnaire; Herzog's interviews and the invention of 'checking up'; the General Education Board grant; the Princeton Radio Research Project (1937, $67,000); Cantril's biography; the argument that the book is continuous with the Bureau's work.

pooley-socolow-2013-slate.title: The myth of the War of the Worlds panic

verified.note: Page opened and read in full (published 28 Oct 2013): Hooper survey of 5,000 households (2 per cent), newspapers and radio, no verified deaths, hospital checks, Cantril's reliance on the AIPO survey and the quoted 'over 100 per cent higher' remark, Campbell's finding on fading coverage, the FCC's informal agreement. Popular version by the same authors as the peer-reviewed IJoC article; independent confirmation comes from Hayes & Battles 2011 and the NPR review of Schwartz 2015.

Page opened: Lasswell 1902-1978; born in Donnellson, Illinois; university scholarship at sixteen; faculty at Chicago and later Yale; died in New York City in 1978; Propaganda Technique (1927) and Politics: Who Gets What, When, How (1936); the 'who says what in which channel to whom with what effect' formula. The page mis-titles the 1927 book 'Propaganda Technique in World War I'; the title is taken from the book itself.

Second, separate reference-work entry on the same site (opened via a fetch tool): born 1902 in Donnellson, Illinois; died 1978; Ph.D. in political science, Chicago; later professor at Yale; policy sciences. Only birth and death years and the broad career are used because the two entries differ on the years of individual posts.

Entry opened (updated 7 April 2025): Cantril (1906-1969), US psychologist; The Invasion from Mars (1940) 'with the assistance of' Hazel Gaudet and Herta Herzog; it prints the script by Howard Koch of Welles's 30 October 1938 broadcast of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds. Dates 1906-1969 agree with Pooley & Socolow 2013.
